claim_records.text: The proposed Meta-Metric-Learner hybrid meta-learning model combines optimization-based and metric-based meta-learning approaches, consisting of a task-specific metric-based learner as a base model and a meta-learner that learns and specifies the base model.
The Meta-Metric-Learner model is able to handle flexible numbers of classes as well as generate more generalized metrics for classification across tasks.

Experiments show the Meta-Metric-Learner approach obtains superior performance in both the standard k-shot N-way few-shot learning setting and a new realistic few-shot setting with flexible class numbers in both single-source and multi-source forms.

Existing optimization-based few-shot learning approaches require task-specific classifiers to be homogeneous-structured to ease parameter prediction, so they can only handle few-shot learning problems where tasks share a uniform number of classes.

Existing metric-based few-shot learning approaches learn one task-invariant metric for all tasks, allowing different numbers of classes but requiring all tasks to come from a similar domain such that a uniform metric works across tasks.
The proposed Meta-Metric-Learner model exploits metric-learning based model to perform classification but learns it via training an optimization-based meta-model.

Because metric-based models are essentially non-parametric models not sensitive to the number of classes, the proposed Meta-Metric-Learner model is able to handle unbalanced classes in meta-train and meta-test sets.
The Meta-Metric-Learner model generates task-specific metrics leveraging the weight prediction of the meta-learner given task instances, so that the metrics adapt better to different tasks.
The learned task-invariant metric of existing metric-based few-shot learning approaches may not generalize well if the tasks diverge, because the optimal metric varies across tasks.
In real-world few-shot learning applications where tasks come from different domains or data sources, there is unlikely to exist a uniform metric suitable for all the tasks.

Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) explicitly trains the initial parameters of a CNN model such that a small number of gradient update steps with a small amount of training data from a new task will produce good generalization performance on that task.
Meta-SGD extends the MAML idea by learning to learn not just the learner initialization, but also the learner update direction and learning rate.

claim_records.text: The proposed adaptive metric learning approach automatically determines the best weighted combination from a set of metrics obtained from meta-training tasks for a newly seen few-shot task.

Extensive quantitative evaluations on real-world sentiment analysis and dialog intent classification datasets show the proposed method performs favorably against state-of-the-art few-shot learning algorithms in terms of predictive accuracy.

The proposed few-shot learning framework uses a task-clustering approach, with an initial task clustering algorithm based on matrix completion followed by a task-clustering-based few-shot learning method.
Directly using transfer performance for task clustering requires conducting source-target transfer learning O(n²) times, where n is the number of meta-training tasks.
For over 1000 diverse meta-training tasks, evaluating the full transfer performance matrix requires over 1 million entries, which is unacceptably slow.

Estimated cross-task transfer performance scores are often unreliable due to small data size or label noise, and large numbers of uncertain values can mislead the clustering algorithm to output an incorrect task partition.
The proposed matrix completion-based task clustering algorithm randomly samples task pairs to evaluate S_ij and S_ji scores to address the large number of required transfer evaluations.
The proposed matrix completion-based task clustering algorithm keeps only task pairs (i,j) with consistent S_ij and S_ji scores to address unreliable entries and asymmetry issues.

Previous few-shot learning works mainly considered image domains such as Omniglot and ImageNet, where tasks are sampled from a single data collection and are thus related, allowing use of a common meta-model for all few-shot tasks.
In enterprise AI cloud service text classification scenarios, submitted client tasks are significantly diverse, so a common metric is insufficient to handle all tasks.

claim_records.text: Deep metric learning methods for few-shot image classification classify unseen samples by their distances to few seen samples in a learned deep neural network embedding space, avoiding overfitting to few training images and achieving state-of-the-art performance.

The review categorizes deep metric learning methods for few-shot image classification from 2018 to 2022 into three groups corresponding to three metric learning stages: learning feature embeddings, learning class representations, and learning distance measures.

In few-shot classification, the metric is learned on the base dataset, and query images of novel classes are classified by computing their distances to novel support images with the learned measure, followed by a distance-based classifier such as k-nearest neighbors.

fact_fields.method: Supervised metric learning for few-shot classification

claim_records.text: Early few-shot metric learning methods such as Siamese Network and Matching Network classify a query sample by measuring and comparing its distance to support samples, but scarce support samples have limited capacity to represent the novel class.
Class prototypes used in few-shot metric learning can be constructed by simple or weighted average of feature embeddings, or learned end-to-end to improve representation ability.

Zhang et al. proposed a variational Bayesian framework for few-shot learning that uses Kullback-Leibler divergence to measure sample distance, and computes query class assignment confidence by estimating each class distribution via a neural network.

fact_fields.method: Variational Bayesian framework for few-shot learning

claim_records.text: Simon et al. proposed Deep Subspace Network (DSN), which represents each class using a low-dimensional subspace constructed from support samples via singular value decomposition, and classifies queries via nearest subspace classifier using Euclidean distance between the query and its projection onto the class-specific subspace.
The Deep Subspace Network method is more robust to noises and outliers than the Prototypical Network.
Few-shot classification aims to learn a classification rule from typically 1-5 labeled examples per new class.
The biggest challenge in few-shot classification is a high risk of model overfitting to the few labeled training samples.

Metric learning methods for few-shot classification learn feature embeddings and/or distance/similarity measures, and classify unseen samples based on distance to labeled samples or class representations, with same-class samples expected to be close and different-class samples far apart in the embedding space.

claim_records.text: The Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot (UAFS) image classification framework models uncertainty of query-prototype similarity and performs uncertainty-aware optimization.

For a query sample xi and N prototypes in the support set, each query-prototype pair is treated as a node and a graph-based model is employed to jointly infer the similarity uncertainty σi,j for each query-prototype pair.

The similarity between a query feature zi and a prototype feature cj (where j = 1, · · · , N) is modeled as a distribution (probabilistic similarity) rather than a scalar, based on graph-based similarity uncertainty estimation, to alleviate the influence of observation noises on the query-prototype pair similarity.
The network is optimized with similarity-based classification losses which exploit the estimated similarity uncertainty.

The proposed Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot framework for image classification models uncertainty of the similarities of query-support pairs and performs uncertainty-aware optimization by converting observed similarities to probabilistic representations and incorporating them to the loss for more effective optimization.
A graph-based model is utilized to estimate the uncertainty of query-support pairs in order to jointly consider the similarities between a query and the prototypes in a support set.
Extensive experiments show the proposed Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot method brings significant improvements on top of a strong baseline and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

In few-shot image classification, the set of category-specific prototypes (computed by averaging feature embeddings of support samples of each category) acts as a similarity-based classifier to identify the category of a query sample by finding the nearest prototype over the support set in the embedding space.

During training for few-shot image classification, the logit vector (classification probability) for a query sample is obtained by feeding the similarities between the query sample and the prototypes to a SoftMax function.

For few-shot image classification, the network has different uncertainties on the calculated similarities of different query-prototype pairs, and an observed similarity of a query-prototype pair (being a one time sampling) suffers from observation noise, where higher uncertainty corresponds to less reliable estimated similarity.

For each few-shot task during optimization, the number of experienced query-prototype pairs is limited, so the side effect of observation noises due to high uncertainty limits optimization, making uncertainty modeling especially vital for few-shot learning with limited samples.

For each query-prototype pair, the observed feature similarity between the query and the prototype is converted from a deterministic scalar to a distribution, with the variance of this distribution characterizing the uncertainty of the observed similarity.

claim_records.text: Existing metric-based few-shot classification algorithms often fail to generalize to unseen domains due to large discrepancy of the feature distribution across domains.

The proposed approach uses feature-wise transformation layers that augment image features using affine transforms to simulate various feature distributions under different domains in the training stage.

claim_records.text: A learning-to-learn approach is applied to search for the hyper-parameters of the feature-wise transformation layers to capture variations of feature distributions under different domains.
Extensive experiments and ablation studies under the domain generalization setting are conducted using five few-shot classification datasets: mini-ImageNet, CUB, Cars, Places, and Plantae.

Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed feature-wise transformation layer is applicable to various metric-based models, and provides consistent improvements on few-shot classification performance under domain shift.

Metric-based few-shot classification methods consist of a feature encoder and a metric function: given an input task with support set (few labeled images) and query set (unlabeled images) from novel classes, the encoder extracts image features, and the metric function takes features of both labeled and unlabeled images as input to predict the category of query images.
Existing metric-based approaches do not generalize well to categories from different domains, as reported by Chen et al. (2019a).
The distributions of image features extracted from tasks in unseen domains are significantly different from those in seen domains.

Unsupervised domain adaptation approaches assume numerous unlabeled images are available in the target domain during training, which may not be realistic in cases such as collecting images of rare bird species.
Existing domain generalization approaches aim at recognizing instances from the same category in the training stage.
During training, the metric function may overfit to feature distributions encoded only from seen domains and thus fail to generalize to unseen domains.

Integrating feature-wise transformation layers that modulate feature activations with affine transformations into the feature encoder allows simulating various distributions of image features during training, improving the generalization ability of the metric function in the testing phase.

claim_records.text: The proposed Region Comparison Network (RCN) is a metric learning based method designed to reveal how few-shot learning works in a neural network and identify specific mutually related regions in query and support set images.
Region Activation Mapping (RAM) is a visualization strategy developed to intuitively explain what RCN has learned by visualizing intermediate variables in the network.
The paper presents a method to generalize interpretability from the task level to the category level, which can be used to find prototypical parts supporting RCN's final classification decisions.
Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that RCN outperforms existing baselines on few-shot image classification.

Few-shot learning is attracting increasing research attention because deep learning models typically require large-scale training data, making it difficult to apply them to tasks with limited available data.
Existing few-shot learning works are grouped into metric-based models and gradient-based models.
Gradient-based few-shot learning methods such as MAML and MetaSGD are model agnostic and can be combined with metric learning models to improve few-shot learning performance.

RCN's final prediction module directly indicates the relationship between final classification decisions and region similarities in the last layer, forming a simple and easily explained linear process compared to attention mechanisms.

claim_records.text: Existing CLIP-based few-shot classification approaches such as CoOp and Tip-Adapter only focus on high-level visual features that are fully aligned with textual features representing the 'Summary' of the image.
Low-level local representations (LRs) are more consistent between seen and unseen samples than high-level representations in few-shot classification.
The proposed Meta-Feature Adaption method (MF-Adapter) combines the complementary strengths of low-level local representations and high-level semantic representations for few-shot classification.
The Meta-Feature Unit (MF-Unit) is a simple yet effective local similarity metric designed to measure category-consistent local context in an inductive manner.
Extensive experiments show that MF-Adapter outperforms state-of-the-art CLIP downstream few-shot classification methods, including on challenging visual classification tasks.
In few-shot classification scenarios where seen images are insufficient, simply adopting the 'pre-training&fine-tuning' paradigm does not produce better results.

MF-Unit is obtained by inductive representation of local feature maps on different scales using sliding windows with different perceptual fields, containing rich local information to represent category-consistent characteristics.

fact_fields.method: MF-Unit construction via multi-scale sliding windows

claim_records.text: MF-Unit is calculated by applying inductive max and mean operations on each sliding window to compress parameters and reduce redundancy, producing category-consistent features containing inductive knowledge.

fact_fields.method: MF-Unit computation via max and mean pooling

claim_records.text: During inference, MF-Adapter first infers test images into MF-Units at different levels and scales, retrieves few-shot knowledge in the MF-Unit space of the support set to get local logits, then combines this with the original CLIP high-level prediction for the final output.
MF-Adapter is the first work to utilize the local similarity of CLIP in few-shot learning.
Comprehensive experiments on 11 widely adopted datasets for few-shot classification show that MF-Adapter achieves state-of-the-art performance compared with previous CLIP-based methods.

claim_records.text: Prototypical networks are proposed for few-shot classification, where a classifier must generalize to new classes not seen in the training set given only a small number of examples of each new class.
Prototypical networks learn a metric space in which classification is performed by computing distances to prototype representations of each class.
Prototypical networks reflect a simpler inductive bias beneficial in the limited-data few-shot learning regime compared to recent approaches, and achieve excellent results.
Analysis shows that some simple design decisions for prototypical networks can yield substantial improvements over recent approaches involving complicated architectural choices and meta-learning.
Prototypical networks extended to zero-shot learning achieve state-of-the-art results on the CU-Birds dataset.

claim_records.text: The subspace representation learning (SRL) framework represents an image by exploiting a subspace in local CNN feature space, and measures similarity between two images according to a weighted subspace distance (WSD).
When K images are available for each class, two types of template subspaces are developed to aggregate K-shot information: the prototypical subspace (PS) and the discriminative subspace (DS).
The SRL framework extends metric learning based techniques from vector to subspace representation.
Using subspace representation can effectively preserve the spatial structure and diversity within an image, unlike most previous works that adopted global vector representation.

The SRL framework demonstrates competitive/superior performance compared to the previous state-of-the-art on three public benchmark datasets: MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet and Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (CUB).

claim_records.text: Previous metric-based few-shot image classification work mainly focuses on image-level feature representations, which cannot effectively estimate a class's distribution due to the scarcity of samples.
Some recent work shows that local descriptor based representations can achieve richer representations than image-level based representations.
Existing local descriptor based works are still based on a less effective instance-level metric, especially a symmetric metric, to measure the relations between query images and support classes.
Given the natural asymmetric relation between a query image and a support class, an asymmetric measure is more suitable for metric-based few-shot learning.
The Asymmetric Distribution Measure (ADM) network calculates a joint local and global asymmetric measure between two multivariate local distributions of queries and classes for few-shot learning.
A task-aware Contrastive Measure Strategy (CMS) is proposed to further enhance the measure function of the ADM network.
On miniImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 3.02% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.
On tieredImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 1.56% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.

claim_records.text: RankDNN casts relevance ranking for image retrieval as binary ranking relation classification.
Ranking relation classification is sample efficient and domain agnostic in comparison to image classification.
The core component of RankDNN is a simple MLP that takes as input an image triplet encoded as the difference between two vector-Kronecker products and outputs a binary relevance ranking order.
RankMLP can be built on top of any state-of-the-art feature extractors.
RankDNN can be flexibly fused with other post-processing methods.
During meta test, RankDNN ranks support images according to their similarity with query samples and assigns each query sample the class label of its nearest neighbor.
RankDNN can effectively improve the performance of its baselines based on a variety of backbones.
RankDNN outperforms previous state-of-the-art algorithms on multiple few-shot learning benchmarks including miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, Caltech-UCSD Birds, and CIFAR-FS.
Experiments on the cross-domain challenge demonstrate the superior transferability of RankDNN.
RankDNN provides a new perspective on few-shot learning and is complementary to state-of-the-art methods.

claim_records.text: Traditional metric-based few-shot classification methods typically rely on a single distance value between the query feature and support feature, thereby overlooking the contribution of shallow features.

The proposed approach uses a multi-output embedding network that maps samples into distinct feature spaces, extracting feature vectors at different stages to capture both global and abstract features.
Employing a self-attention mechanism improves the refinement of features at each stage, leading to more robust representations and improved overall performance.
Assigning learnable weights to each stage of the multi-output embedding network significantly improved performance and results.
Comprehensive evaluations were conducted on the MiniImageNet and FC100 datasets in the 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot scenarios.
Cross-domain tasks across eight benchmark datasets achieved high accuracy in the testing domains for the proposed method.
The evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in comparison to state-of-the-art approaches.

claim_records.text: Existing metric-learning few-shot image classification methods that use a measure at only the image feature level may not be effective enough to generalize from base to novel classes when using only a few images.

The proposed multi-level correlation network (MLCN) for few-shot image classification tackles the limited effectiveness of image-feature-level-only measures by effectively capturing local information.
MLCN includes a self-correlation module and a cross-correlation module that learn the semantic correspondence relation of local information based on learned representations.
MLCN includes a pattern-correlation module that captures the pattern of fine-grained images and finds relevant structural patterns between base classes and novel classes.
Extensive experiments and analysis show the effectiveness of the proposed MLCN method on four widely-used few-shot image classification benchmarks.

claim_records.text: HyperShot is proposed as a fusion of kernels and the hypernetwork paradigm for few-shot learning.
HyperShot switches classification module parameters depending on the task's embedding, rather than applying gradient-based adjustment of parameters as reference approaches do.
HyperShot uses a hypernetwork that takes aggregated information from support data and returns classifier parameters handcrafted for the considered problem.
HyperShot introduces a kernel-based representation of support examples delivered to the hypernetwork to create the parameters of the classification module.
HyperShot relies on relations between embeddings of support examples instead of direct feature values provided by backbone models.
The HyperShot approach enables the model to adapt to highly different tasks.

claim_records.text: FewSAR consists of an open-source Python code library of 15 classic methods in three categories for few-shot SAR image classification.
Within the FewSAR benchmark under the same setting, metric learning methods achieve the best classification accuracy among the three method categories.
Within the FewSAR benchmark, meta-learning methods and fine-tuning methods perform poorly on few-shot SAR images, which is primarily attributed to the bias of existing datasets.
The lack of a unified benchmark for SAR target image classification is a key reason for the slower progress in SAR target image classification compared to rapid development of visible light datasets.

The practice of SAR target image classification researchers reporting new results on their own datasets and experimental setup leads to inefficiency in result comparison and impedes further progress of the area.

claim_records.text: The proposed Siamese Transformer Network (STN) uses two parallel branch networks built on the pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture to extract global and local features respectively.
The STN implementation uses the ViT-Small network architecture, with branch networks initialized using pre-trained model parameters obtained through self-supervised learning.
In STN, Euclidean distance is applied to global features and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence is applied to local features to compute feature similarity.
STN integrates global and local feature similarity metrics by first applying L2 normalization to each metric, then weighting the normalized results to obtain the final similarity score.
During the training phase of STN, a meta-learning approach is adopted to fine-tune the entire network.

Extensive experiments show that the STN framework achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines on four popular few-shot classification benchmarks in both 5-shot and 1-shot scenarios.

claim_records.text: Network intrusion detection systems face significant challenges in identifying emerging attack patterns, especially when limited data samples are available.

The MSPL framework operates across multiple metric spaces—Euclidean, Cosine, Chebyshev, and Wasserstein distances—integrated through a constrained weighting scheme to enhance embedding robustness and improve pattern recognition.
The MSPL framework leverages Polyak-averaged prototype generation to stabilize the learning process and effectively adapt to rare and zero-day attacks.
The MSPL framework uses an episodic training paradigm to ensure balanced representation across diverse attack classes, enabling robust generalization.

Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that MSPL outperforms traditional approaches in detecting low-profile and novel attack types, establishing it as a robust solution for zero-day attack detection.

claim_records.text: The proposed LaSO method combines pairs of given examples in feature space to synthesize feature vectors whose corresponding label sets are obtained via set operations on the label sets of the input pairs.
The proposed LaSO method is capable of producing a synthesized sample containing the intersection, union, or set-difference of labels present in two input samples.
The set operations implemented by LaSO generalize to labels that are unseen during training.

Experiments demonstrate promising label-set manipulation capabilities of the proposed LaSO approach, evaluated directly using classification and retrieval metrics, and in the context of data augmentation for multi-label few-shot learning.
The proposed LaSO method compares favorably to all common baselines on the newly proposed benchmark for multi-label few-shot learning.
Current existing sample synthesis approaches for few-shot learning only address the scenario of a single category label per image.
Example synthesis is identified as one of the leading methods to tackle the few-shot learning problem where only a small number of samples per class are available.
The proposed LaSO method enables performing augmentation on examples of novel categories, facilitating multi-label few-shot classifier learning.

claim_records.text: Most existing webly supervised learning (WSL) methods focus on learning noise-robust models from web images while neglecting the performance drop caused by domain differences between web data and real-world data.
The proposed FoPro (Few-shot guided Prototypical) representation learning method only needs a few labeled real-world examples and can significantly improve performance in the real-world domain.
FoPro initializes each class center with few-shot real-world data as the 'realistic' prototype.
FoPro narrows the intra-class distance between web instances and 'realistic' prototypes via contrastive learning.
FoPro measures image-prototype distance with a learnable metric, polishes prototypes using adjacent high-quality web images, and uses prototypes to remove distant out-of-distribution samples.
In experiments, FoPro is trained on web datasets with guidance from a few real-world examples and evaluated on real-world datasets.
FoPro achieves state-of-the-art performance on three fine-grained datasets and two large-scale datasets.
Compared with existing WSL methods under the same few-shot settings, FoPro still excels in real-world generalization.
FoPro code is publicly available at https://github.com/yuleiqin/fopro.

claim_records.text: The proposed DN4 framework achieves the largest absolute improvement of 17% over the next best related state-of-the-art method on benchmark few-shot learning datasets.

DN4 replaces the image-level feature based measure in the final layer with a local descriptor based image-to-class measure conducted online via k-nearest neighbor search over deep local descriptors of convolutional feature maps.

DN4 learns optimal deep local descriptors for the image-to-class measure and leverages the higher efficiency of this measure under example scarcity, enabled by the exchangeability of visual patterns across images in the same class.

claim_records.text: The proposed generative dual adversarial network for generalized zero-shot learning unifies visual-to-semantic mapping, semantic-to-visual mapping, and metric learning in a single framework.

The proposed model comprises a feature generator that produces visual features from class embeddings, a regressor that maps visual features back to class embeddings, and a discriminator that evaluates closeness between image features and class embeddings.

claim_records.text: The proposed patch-driven relational refinement learns cache adapter weights from intra-image patch dependencies rather than treating an image embedding as a monolithic vector.

The introduced relational gated graph attention network constructs a patch graph and performs edge-aware attention to emphasize informative inter-patch interactions, producing context-enriched patch embeddings.
A learnable multi-aggregation pooling composes context-enriched patch embeddings into compact, task-discriminative representations that better align cache keys with target few-shot classes.
The proposed graph refinement is used only during training to distil relational structure into the cache, incurring no additional inference cost beyond standard cache lookup.
Final predictions are obtained by a residual fusion of cache similarity scores with CLIP zero-shot logits.

claim_records.text: Few-shot Cosine Transformer (FS-CT) obtains the relational map between supports and queries for few-shot tasks.

FS-CT consists of a learnable prototypical embedding network to obtain categorical representations from support samples with hard cases, and a transformer encoder to effectively achieve the relational map from two different support and query samples.
Cosine Attention, a more robust and stable attention module, improves FS-CT performance from 5% to over 20% in accuracy compared to the default scaled dot-product mechanism.
FS-CT performs competitive results in mini-ImageNet, CUB-200, and CIFAR-FS on 1-shot learning and 5-shot learning tasks across backbones and few-shot configurations.
A custom few-shot dataset for Yoga pose recognition is developed to demonstrate the potential of the FS-CT algorithm for practical application.
FS-CT with cosine attention is a lightweight, simple few-shot algorithm applicable for a wide range of applications including healthcare, medical, and security surveillance.
The official implementation code of Few-shot Cosine Transformer is available at https://github.com/vinuni-vishc/Few-Shot-Cosine-Transformer.

claim_records.text: HelixFormer is a Transformer-based double-helix model designed to perform cross-image object semantic relation mining in a bidirectional and symmetrical manner for few-shot fine-grained image classification.
HelixFormer consists of two core steps: the Relation Mining Process (RMP) across different branches, and the Representation Enhancement Process (REP) within each individual branch.

The RMP step of HelixFormer enables each branch to extract fine-grained object-level Cross-image Semantic Relation Maps (CSRMs) using information from the other branch, to support better cross-image interaction in semantically related local object regions.

The REP step of HelixFormer uses CSRMs to strengthen extracted features for discovered semantically-related local regions in each branch, improving the model's ability to distinguish subtle fine-grained object feature differences.
Experiments on five public fine-grained benchmarks show HelixFormer achieves better performance over most state-of-the-art methods under both 1-shot and 5-shot few-shot scenarios.

claim_records.text: In few-shot learning, conventional pooled global features are likely to lose useful local characteristics under low-data regimes.

Existing deep descriptor-based FSL methods take all deep descriptors from neural networks into consideration, ignoring that some descriptors are useless for classification due to limited receptive field.
Task-irrelevant deep descriptors can be misleading, and multiple aggregative descriptors from background clutter can overwhelm the object's presence in FSL.

The proposed approach establishes a Mutual Nearest Neighbor (MNN) relation to explicitly select query descriptors most relevant to each task and discard less relevant ones from aggregative clutters in FSL.

The proposed Discriminative Mutual Nearest Neighbor Neural Network (DMN4) for FSL outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on both fine-grained and generalized datasets per extensive experiments.

claim_records.text: In meta-learning for few-shot classification, the number of labeled examples per category (shot number) used during meta-training impacts recognition performance at meta-test time.
Generally, the shot number used in meta-training should match the shot number used in meta-testing to obtain the best few-shot classification performance.
The paper introduces a theoretical analysis of the impact of shot number on Prototypical Networks, a state-of-the-art few-shot classification method.
The paper proposes a simple method derived from its theoretical analysis that is robust to the choice of shot number used during meta-training, a crucial hyperparameter.

fact_fields.method: proposed simple method derived from theoretical analysis

claim_records.text: The proposed model trained for an arbitrary meta-training shot number shows strong performance across different values of meta-testing shot numbers.
The proposed approach is experimentally demonstrated on different few-shot classification benchmarks.

claim_records.text: The paper introduces Prototypical Random Walk Networks (PRWN), a semi-supervised few-shot learning (SS-FSL) approach built on top of Prototypical Networks (PN).
PRWN uses a developed random walk semi-supervised loss that enables the network to learn representations that are compact and well-separated.

Compact and well-separated class representations can be achieved by modeling the prototypical random walk notion without needing additional graph-NN parameters or requiring a transductive setting where a collective test set is provided.
The PRWN model outperforms baselines in most benchmarks, with significant improvements in some cases.
PRWN trained with 40% of the data as labeled compares competitively against fully supervised Prototypical Networks trained on 100% of the labels.

In the 1-shot mini-Imagenet case, PRWN trained with 40% labeled data achieves 50.89% accuracy, outperforming fully supervised Prototypical Networks trained on 100% labels which achieve 49.4% accuracy.

fact_fields.method: Prototypical Random Walk Networks (PRWN) vs fully supervised Prototypical Networks

claim_records.text: The PRWN random walk semi-supervised loss is resistant to distractors (unlabeled data that does not belong to any of the training classes), reflecting robustness to labeled/unlabeled class distribution mismatch.
An associated GitHub page for the work is available at https://prototypical-random-walk.github.io.

claim_records.text: Boundary patches corresponding to pixels located at the boundary of objects in hyperspectral images are hard to classify, as they are mixed with multi-class spectral information.

The proposed APNT method takes the prototype network as the backbone and adopts a transformer as feature extractor to learn pixel-to-pixel relations and apply different attentions to different pixels.

APNT randomly mixes up two hyperspectral image patches to imitate boundary patches and uses the synthetic patches for training, to enlarge the number of hard training samples and enhance their diversity.
APNT follows the TransMix data augmentation technique, using the attention returned by the transformer to mix up the labels of two patches to generate better labels for synthetic patches.
The proposed APNT method demonstrates state-of-the-art performance and better robustness for few-shot hyperspectral image classification compared with existing methods in experiments.

claim_records.text: Proto-CLIP adapts image and text encoder embeddings from CLIP in a joint fashion using few-shot examples, and uses the embeddings from the two encoders to compute respective prototypes of image classes for classification.
During adaptation, aligning the image and text prototypes of corresponding classes is beneficial for few-shot classification due to reinforced contributions from both types of prototypes.
Proto-CLIP has both training-free and fine-tuned variants.
The effectiveness of Proto-CLIP is demonstrated by experiments on benchmark datasets for few-shot learning, as well as in real-world robot perception scenarios.
